title: A randomized controlled trial on effects of the Transcendental Meditation program on blood pressure, psychological distress, and coping in young adults.
authors: Nidich SI, Rainforth MV, Haaga DA, Hagelin J, Salerno JW, Travis F, Tanner M, Gaylord-King C, Grosswald S, Schneider RH.
age: University students, mean 25.5; no youth-only upper limit
finding: Overall blood-pressure differences were not statistically significant. The hypertension-risk subgroup had larger reductions, alongside reported improvements in distress and coping. Subgroup cardiovascular findings do not demonstrate a general youth mental-health effect.
limitation: About 30% missing posttests, inactive control, three-month duration and mixed-age student sample. Overall BP differences were nonsignificant; subgroup BP finding is not universal hypertension prevention.
labImplication: Consider voluntary meditation as a component to evaluate; do not claim the lab prevents hypertension.

authors: Klimes-Dougan B, Chong LS, Samikoglu A, Thai M, Amatya P, Cullen KR, Lim KO.

finding: Morning cortisol measures changed in favour of TM, but cortisol responses to the laboratory social stress test did not differ significantly. This is a small mechanistic pilot rather than evidence of a broad clinical benefit.

labImplication: If stress biology is studied in the PhD, separate awakening cortisol from acute stress reactivity and subjective stress.

authors: Gomes A, Vieira Dos Santos J, Vieira LS.

labImplication: Retain null findings; do not promise anxiety or resilience gains from TM.

title: The impact of sound intervention on sleep quality and stress levels in college students: a randomized controlled trial.
authors: Hou H, Wang J, Yue X.
topics: Music / creative participation; Sound / brain entrainment
age: 18–25 years, college students with poor sleep; diagnosed psychiatric disorders excluded.
finding: Self-reported sleep and stress improved with the audio interventions; stress reductions favoured beats plus music. Cortisol showed a time effect but no group difference. The design does not isolate beats from music or expectancy.
limitation: Small sample, no music-only active control, unblinded self-reports and one daily cortisol time point.
labImplication: Test accessible audio experiences with appropriate active comparators and immediate stress measures; avoid endocrine claims.

title: The effects of music & auditory beat stimulation on anxiety: A randomized clinical trial.
authors: Mallik A, Russo FA.
topics: Music / creative participation; Sound / brain entrainment
age: Adults over 18; arm means approximately 26–31, with no separate 16–24 estimate.
finding: In the moderate-trait-anxiety subgroup, some anxiety reductions favoured combined audio and music. Treatment separation was weaker for high-trait-anxiety participants. The population and subgroup analyses limit transfer to a youth academy.
limitation: Open-label, self-reported acute outcomes, subgroup comparisons, commercial technology involvement and no youth-specific estimate.
labImplication: A rationale for a controlled short-term listening experiment, not evidence that beats add benefit for all young people.

title: The Efficacy of Binaural Beats as a Stress-buffering Technique.
authors: Kelton K, Weaver TL, Willoughby L, Kaufman D, Santowski A.
journal: Alternative therapies in health and medicine
finding: The beat condition did not significantly reduce subjective stress or change HRV during initial listening. A later HRV difference during the stress task favoured the beat condition, suggesting a physiological signal without demonstrated perceived-stress benefit.
limitation: Pilot with mixed endpoints; full allocation, masking and attrition methods were not accessible.
labImplication: Measure felt stress directly rather than substituting an HRV change for a participant benefit.

title: Trauma-focused treatments for refugee children and adolescents with PTSD: a three-arm randomized controlled trial comparing the efficacy of EMDR and KIDNET versus a waitlist control group (the KIEM study).
authors: Velu ME, de Roos C, van der Aa N, Jongedijk R, Lindauer R, Mooren T.
journal: Child and adolescent psychiatry and mental health
finding: Both treatments reduced clinician-rated PTSD more than waiting (EMDR d=1.31; KIDNET d=0.94). EMDR had a modest advantage on clinician-rated severity over KIDNET, without consistent superiority on other outcomes. Parent-reported results differed from child/clinician reports.

labImplication: Outreach locations, language support and culturally informed engagement provide a concrete access model; therapy requires its clinical delivery and cannot be equated with an audiovisual experience.

title: Peer-delivered combined EMD and imagery rescripting for traumatized Chinese university students: a RCT.
authors: Fan H, Zhang J, Wang Y, Yang K, Wang Y, Yang X.
age: Chinese university students; exact age range requires table verification.
finding: Depression, anxiety and self-efficacy group-by-time effects were not significant. Resilience maintenance favoured the combined intervention on a narrower comparison. EMD here is restricted processing combined with imagery rescripting, not standard full-protocol EMDR.
limitation: Randomized/analyzed denominator discrepancy, short follow-up and multiple endpoints. Mediation does not prove a causal mechanism.
labImplication: Highlights supervision and referral design, while preventing claims that peers delivering EMD established broad symptom efficacy.
holdReason: Resolve denominator and observed age reporting before content approval.

title: Clinical and Cost-Effectiveness of Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Sutton A, Carroll C, Simpson E, Forsyth J, Rayner A, Ren S, Franklin M, Wood E.
age: Children and adolescents, with adolescents defined as 10–19; no isolated 16–24 estimate.
finding: Pooled PTSD symptom effects favoured EMDR over waiting/usual care (SMD 1.57, 95% credible interval 0.07–3.21). Two direct comparisons did not establish superiority over trauma-focused CBT. Economic evidence was sparse.
limitation: All clinical studies were judged moderate or high risk of bias; wide uncertainty and little long-term evidence. Reviews and their included trials are not independent corroborating samples.
labImplication: Supports access to established trauma-focused clinical options and an explicit evidence-gap agenda, not a guaranteed lab outcome.

title: Psychological Interventions for Pediatric Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
authors: Hoppen TH, Wessarges L, Jehn M, Mutz J, Kip A, Schlechter P, Meiser-Stedman R, Morina N.
age: Children and adolescents aged 19 or younger.
finding: EMDR and other interventions reduced PTSD more than passive controls at treatment end. Trauma-focused CBT had the most consistent evidence across comparators and follow-up periods; longer-term EMDR evidence remained limited.
limitation: Network comparisons rely on comparability across heterogeneous trials; results do not isolate ages 16–24.
labImplication: Design referral options around the full evidence base, rather than making EMDR the only trauma pathway.

authors: de Roos C, van der Oord S, Zijlstra B, Lucassen S, Perrin S, Emmelkamp P, de Jongh A.
journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines

finding: Reported greater reductions in stress, state anxiety and hair cortisol; 71% of intervention respondents found it helpful.
limitation: Unblinded self-report, inactive comparator, mostly female, course participation recruitment, missing hair samples and unusable HRV. No economic evaluation supports the paper's broader cost-effectiveness language.
labImplication: Direct age fit for a pilot of credentialed group music therapy and short-term stress measurement, not evidence of whole-lab or electronic production efficacy.

title: Effectiveness of training programs based on mindfulness in reducing psychological distress and promoting well-being in medical students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: da Silva CCG, Bolognani CV, Amorim FF, Imoto AM.
age: Medical students over 18; mixed adult ages
finding: Small immediate stress effect SMD −0.29 (95% CI −0.56 to −0.02); immediate wellbeing difference not significant. Anxiety/depression/resilience certainty low.

finding: Perceived stress improved (ITT β −2.31, p=.03); depression, anxiety and mindfulness did not differ significantly.

title: The effectiveness of peer support from a person with lived experience of mental health challenges for young people with anxiety and depression: a systematic review.
authors: Simmons MB, Cartner S, MacDonald R, Whitson S, Bailey A, Brown E.
design: Systematic review of controlled peer-support interventions
finding: Some depression/anxiety or negative-affect benefits, but most studies targeted other conditions and the evidence was limited and heterogeneous.
